progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: An organism is one living individual; a population is a group of individuals of the same species. Plants consist of cells, and cells contain DNA. Offspring are new individuals produced by reproduction. No chromosome terminology is assumed.
progression.startsWith: A grower copies a strawberry plant with valued fruit characteristics, then encounters a new disease. Follow its rooted offspring to connect reproduction, inherited information and later generations.
progression.stopsAfter: Explain how offspring and inherited DNA connect generations, and use copying versus different inherited combinations to compare asexual and sexual reproduction under stated conditions. Apply the comparison to an untested dry-soil trial without promising a favourable outcome.
progression.nextLesson: Animal reproduction: how sperm and egg meet, and how offspring develop in different animals. Focused plant and other-organism mechanisms. The later plant route explains how a flower produces a seed and how a runner establishes a new plant.

teaching.causalExplanation: A rooted daughter plant is a new individual, so reproduction can provide another generation even though a parent has a limited lifetime. The daughter receives DNA from its parent. In runner reproduction, new cells copy the parent's DNA, so the daughter usually retains very similar inherited information. In a sexual cross, sperm and egg join inside a flower and each contributes DNA. Different reproductive cells can carry different inherited selections, so joining different pairs can produce different offspring combinations even with the same two parents. A copied plant can retain valued inherited characteristics and a shared inherited weakness. Different inherited combinations may give different responses to a changed condition, if the relevant differences are present. Producing offspring permits continuity. Enough offspring still need to survive and reproduce for a population to continue.

flower.prompt: Use case: scientific-educational. Create one isolated botanical teaching illustration of a strawberry (Fragaria x ananassa) flower, in naturalistic fine ink linework and restrained watercolour washes, dark green, pale yellow, muted earth colours. Pure white background, no typography, arrows, panels or decorative frame. Composition: one large recognisable open strawberry flower shown in a slightly oblique front view, five broad white petals with fine veins, small green pointed sepals visible behind, many golden-yellow anthers arranged in a ring, and a distinct central pale-green slightly conical receptacle densely covered with MANY small separate pistils, each with its own ovary and slender style. Attach a short slender pedicel angled down left and one smaller trifoliate strawberry leaf on a neighbouring short petiole at lower left to establish organism context without obscuring the flower. The flower fills around 80 percent of the image; plenty of clear margin. Botanically accurate strawberry anatomy, NOT one large lily-style central ovary, NOT a single central pistil. Do not depict enlarged egg cells, sperm, pollen grains in transit, insects, fruit, roots or a runner. No realistic photographic texture, no heavy solid graphic outlines, no logos. Intended later overlay will point to one of the numerous pistils and show a magnified cell joining model, so keep the centre clear, crisp and anatomically distinguishable. This is physical organism art rather than a rendered infographic.

seedling.prompt: Use case: scientific-educational. Create one isolated botanical teaching illustration of a young strawberry plant grown FROM A SEED, in delicate naturalistic ink linework and restrained green watercolour, on pure white background with no labels, arrows, lettering, panels or decorative frame. Side-on teaching view of a small healthy seedling: two low rounded oval cotyledons on a tiny short stem, above them two small serrated trifoliate true leaves with clear strawberry leaflet shapes emerging from the young crown, and a slender branching root system extending below a thin irregular short earth surface line. Keep the complete leaves, crown and all fine roots within image with generous clear margins; plant fills about 80 percent height, centred. Natural scale relationships. This is a newly established young seed-grown strawberry, no connecting horizontal runner or stolon, no mature fruit, flower or bulb. Do not add a giant visible seed at root, pot, face, pedestal or ornamental landscape. Scientifically plausible young plant illustration, no trait comparison claim.

seed.prompt: Use case: scientific-educational. A single botanical ink-and-watercolour teaching asset on pure white background, with no text, numbers, labels, arrows or frames. Draw ONE greatly magnified strawberry achene, the tiny dry single-seeded fruit normally visible on the outside of a strawberry, shown as a longitudinal opened cutaway. Slender small oval teardrop-shaped achene with muted golden-brown papery outer fruit wall, thin seed coat inside, and a pale cream developing embryo protected inside the seed. The embryo has two small fleshy cotyledons and a short radicle below them; keep structure simplified but botanically plausible for a dicot seed, no bean-sized dark seed or loose pollen grain. Show a removed narrow front window so that the seed and embryo are visibly inside a retaining outer wall, rather than floating outside. Stand alone on white, generous margins, delicate fine botanical hatch lines and gentle watercolour shading. No strawberry fruit flesh, extra seeds, roots emerging out of it, germination sprout, detached parts or magnified cells. It will accompany the sentence 'The developing new plant is inside a seed'; fine structures do not need separate labels. Match naturalistic educational botanical plate style.
